newsitem.title: UK: Blair continues UK revolution with legislation.
newsitem.headline: Blair continues UK revolution with legislation.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair sets out on Wednesday the centrepiece of his blueprint to transform Britain, unveiling a hefty legislative programme for the first session of parliament since his Labour Party won the May 1 election.
Labour, which has "hit the ground running" since ending the Conservatives' 18-year spell in office, will announce plans to push more than 20 bills through parliament over the next 17 months.
Government sources said these bills will deal mainly with bread-and-butter issues -- education, health, crime and the introduction of a national minimum wage.
But the programme is also expected to include some of the most radical constitutional reform in Britain for decades.
Blair has announced plans to set up mini-parliaments for Scotland and Wales and to bring in Britain's first law protecting personal privacy which may address widespread concern about media intrusion.
The first Labour election win since 1974 has galvanised politics and policy-making in under two weeks.
Just four days after taking office, finance minister Gordon Brown astonished financial markets by giving freedom to Britain's central bank, the Bank of England, to set official interest rates.
Ministers set out a fresh approach to relations with Britain's European Union partners and Foreign Secretary Robin Cook has pledged a more moral foreign policy, based on regard for human rights.

"There is a lot of optimism out there (following Labour's victory), but there is a lot of work to be done in here," aides quoted Blair as telling last Thursday's cabinet meeting at which the parliamentary programme was agreed.

The programme will be formally announced by Queen Elizabeth (eds: 1030 GMT) in a glittering ceremony in the House of Lords, parliament's upper house. Members last week swore in speaker Betty Boothroyd and new colleagues in the 659-seat House of Commons.
Blair's aides say they will be ready to produce drafts of the first bills within days.

These will include ones to allow referendums to be held on the setting up of the Scottish and Welsh parliaments; to approve the increased powers for the Bank of England; to cut class sizes in primary schools; and to free local councils to spend money sitting in their acccounts to build public housing.
But the passage of these bills may be delayed by the government's need to get a Finance Bill through parliament.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Brown will announce details of the bill, expected to include a five billion pound ($8 billion) one-off tax on "excess profits" of utility companies privatised by the Conservatives, in a budget, probably on June 10.
The crowded programme will be a marked contrast with the more modest "Queen's speeches" produced in recent years by the Conservatives under John Major.
As its majority was whittled away by defections and by-election defeats, Major's government became reluctant to propose controversial legislation for fear of defeat.

With an overall majority of 179 seats in the lower House of Commons, and the opposition Conservatives focusing on the election of a new leader to replace John Major, Blair should have little trouble in getting his legislation passed.
